name: Cubic polynomial
description: A cubic: rules exact for degree 3 (Simpson, Boole, Gauss n ≥ 2) give it exactly.

name: Exponential
description: Smooth and positive; every rule shows its textbook convergence order.

name: Sine on [0, π]
description: One arch of the sine; f′(π/3) = 1/2.

name: Runge function
description: Complex poles at ±i/5 near the interval slow down polynomial-based rules.

name: Square root
description: Singular derivative at x = 0: rules of order ≥ 2 drop to h^{1.5} (Riemann sums keep h).

name: Gaussian
description: The bell curve; the exact integral needs the error function erf.

name: Oscillatory sine
description: Five periods on [0, π]; the exact integral is 0 by symmetry.

name: Derivative of arctan
description: Integrates to π/4: the classic way to compute π by quadrature.

name: Absolute value with a kink
description: A kink at x = 0.3: quadrature loses its order; stencils that straddle it fail.

name: Knapsack, 10 items
description: 10 weakly correlated items (seed 7), capacity = half the total weight. Greedy by value/weight ratio finds 172; the optimum is 173.

name: Knapsack, 20 items
description: 20 weakly correlated items (seed 3), capacity = half the total weight. Greedy finds 397; the optimum is 407 (2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶ subsets for brute force).

name: Greedy trap
description: The small item has the best value/weight ratio, so greedy packs it first and then only one large item fits: greedy = 53, best single item = 50, optimum = 100. Even the 'best single item' fix stays near the ½-approximation bound.

name: 12 cities on a circle
description: Regular 12-gon of radius 40 centered at (50, 50), city order shuffled (seed 12). The optimum is the polygon perimeter 960·sin(π/12) ≈ 248.466.

name: 4 × 4 grid
description: A 4 × 4 grid with spacing 10, city order shuffled (seed 16). Every edge has length ≥ 10 and a boustrophedon cycle uses only length-10 edges: optimum = 160. Many optimal tours exist (ties everywhere).

name: 15 random cities
description: 15 cities with integer coordinates drawn uniformly from {0, …, 100}² (seed 15). Optimum ≈ 399.126.

name: 20 clustered cities
description: Four clusters of five cities (integer offsets in [−10, 10] around fixed centers, seed 21). Good tours visit each cluster once. Optimum ≈ 280.944.

name: Quadratic over the unit disk
description: The unconstrained minimizer (2, 1) lies outside the unit disk, so the constraint is active: the solution is the boundary point (2, 1)/√5 where the level circle of f touches the disk, with multiplier λ⋆ = √5 − 1.

name: Rosenbrock in the disk x² + y² ≤ 2
description: The Rosenbrock minimizer (1, 1) lies exactly on the circle x² + y² = 2. The constraint is active with multiplier λ⋆ = 0 (weakly active: strict complementarity fails), so penalty and barrier methods approach (1, 1) without the constraint pushing back. Rosenbrock is not convex: det ∇²f = 400 − 80000(y − x²), so ∇²f is indefinite where y > x² + 1/200 and Newton steps there need a Hessian modification.

name: Rosenbrock in the unit disk
description: Rosenbrock's banana valley cut off by the unit circle (the classic example of MATLAB's fmincon documentation). The minimizer (0.7864, 0.6177) lies on the circle where the valley meets it, with multiplier λ⋆ ≈ 0.1215.

name: Quadratic in a box
description: A coupled convex quadratic whose unconstrained minimizer (2, 0) lies outside the box [−1, 1]². Only the bound x ≤ 1 is active at the solution (1, ½); clipping (2, 0) to the box would give the wrong point (1, 0).

name: Quadratic on a line
description: The textbook Lagrange-multiplier example: the solution (2/3, 1/3) is where an ellipse x² + 2y² = const touches the line x + y = 1; ∇f = (4/3)(1, 1) is parallel to the line's normal, with multiplier ν⋆ = −4/3. The default start lies on the line.

name: Hock–Schittkowski 21
description: Hock & Schittkowski (1981) test problem 21: a convex quadratic with one general linear inequality and bounds. Only the bound x ≥ 2 is active at (2, 0). The published start (−1, −1) is infeasible; the default start (10, 10) is strictly feasible so that interior-point methods can use it.

name: Quadratic in a wedge of two half-planes
description: Two linear inequalities form an unbounded wedge; the unconstrained minimizer (2, 3/2) lies outside it and the solution is the corner (2/3, 2/3) where both constraints are active with multipliers 4/3 and 2/3.

name: Linear function on the unit circle
description: A linear objective on a nonlinear equality constraint (a nonconvex feasible set). The Lagrangian's curvature 2ν⋆I comes only from the constraint. The point (1/√2, 1/√2) is also a KKT point (ν = −1/√2), but it is the maximizer.

name: Mishra's bird (constrained)
description: A multimodal benchmark (Mishra 2006) restricted to a disk. It has five local minimizers: three interior ones (including the global one) and two on the boundary circle with an active constraint. Local methods find whichever basin they start in.

name: Runge function, 11 equispaced nodes
description: Runge's example: the degree-10 interpolant on equispaced nodes oscillates wildly near ±1 (max error ≈ 1.9), and the error grows with the degree.

name: Runge function, 11 Chebyshev nodes
description: The same function sampled at the roots of T₁₁: the node polynomial is minimal in the max norm, and the interpolation error converges as the degree grows.

name: sin x, 9 equispaced samples
description: A smooth, analytic function: every interpolant converges quickly.

name: Unit step (discontinuous)
description: Monotone data with a jump: polynomials and cubic splines overshoot (Gibbs-like), while PCHIP and the linear spline stay monotone. The jump has height 1, so the sup-norm error of any continuous interpolant is at least 1/2; the 200-point error grid has no point at x = 0, so the reported max errors of the splines are a little lower (about 0.46–0.48).

name: Noisy line
description: Twenty points on a line with Gaussian noise (Mulberry32 seed 42, Box–Muller).

name: Noisy parabola
description: Twenty-five points on a parabola with Gaussian noise (seed 7): a line underfits, degree 2 fits, high degrees overfit.

name: Anscombe's quartet I
description: Anscombe (1973), set I, in the published order: the well-behaved member of the quartet. OLS gives ŷ = 3.0001 + 0.5001x with R² = 0.6665.

name: Line with two gross outliers
description: A clean line (seed 11) with y₅ raised by 15 and y₁₆ lowered by 20: ordinary least squares is pulled away, while Huber, LAD and Theil–Sen stay within the noise of the least-squares line through the 18 clean points.

name: Exponential growth
description: Multiplicative noise on an exponential (seed 3): a straight line fits badly; a line fitted to log y recovers log 2 and 0.3.

name: Exponential decay fit
description: Fit y = a·exp(−b t) to 15 noisy samples of 2.5·exp(−1.3 t) (σ = 0.05). A small-residual problem: Gauss–Newton converges fast near the solution.

name: Rosenbrock (least squares)
description: Rosenbrock's function written as residuals (MGH problem 1); f is half the usual Rosenbrock value. J is square with det J = 10, so Gauss–Newton is Newton's method for r(x) = 0: the full step (no line search) converges in two steps from (−1.2, 1), via (1, −3.84). With Armijo backtracking the first full step is rejected (f rises from 12.1 to 1171), and the damped iteration takes 10 steps.

name: Circle fit (known radius)
description: Find the center of a circle of known radius 2 from 12 noisy points on a 120° arc. The arc is short, so the mirror image of the true center across the arc is a second, worse local minimum; which one a method finds depends on x₀.

name: Michaelis–Menten (Puromycin)
description: Fit the Michaelis–Menten law v = V S/(K + S) to the classic Puromycin (treated) enzyme-kinetics data of Bates & Watts (1988); start (205, 0.08) as in the book. V and K differ in scale by ~3000×, so JᵀJ is badly conditioned (κ ≈ 1.7·10⁶ at the solution).

name: 2×2 SPD system (Shewchuk)
description: Shewchuk's 2×2 example: eigenvalues 2 and 7 (κ₂ = 3.5). Its solution minimizes φ(x) = ½xᵀAx − bᵀx, so iterates can be drawn on the elliptical contours of φ. ρ(T_J) = √2/3 ≈ 0.471, ρ(T_GS) = 2/9.

name: 3×3 diagonally dominant system
description: Strictly diagonally dominant and SPD (κ₂ ≈ 3.37). Every method in the family applies; ρ(T_J) ≈ 0.683 and ρ(T_GS) ≈ 0.177.

name: 1-D Poisson matrix, n = 10
description: The scaled second-difference matrix tridiag(−1, 2, −1) of −u″ = 1 on (0, 1), h = 1/11. Eigenvalues 2 − 2cos(jπ/11), κ₂ ≈ 48.4. ρ(T_J) = cos(π/11) ≈ 0.959, so Jacobi is slow; SOR with ω* = 2/(1 + sin(π/11)) ≈ 1.560 is much faster.

name: Hilbert matrix, n = 5
description: H_ij = 1/(i + j − 1): SPD but κ₂ ≈ 4.77e5, so about 5–6 of the 16 significant digits are lost. `solution` is the exact solution of the exact rational system; the exact solution of the rounded float system differs from it by about 2e-12 (max-norm; the bound κ·u ≈ 5e-11).

name: Zero leading pivot
description: det A = 1, but a₁₁ = 0: Gaussian elimination without row interchanges breaks down at the first stage, while partial pivoting solves it. The zero diagonal entry also makes Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel undefined.

name: Two nearly parallel lines
description: x + y = 2 and x + (1 + δ)y = 2 + δ with δ = 2⁻³⁰: two lines that meet at (1, 1) at an angle of about 4.7e-10 rad (≈ δ/2). κ₂ ≈ 4.3e9, so a relative change of 1e-10 in b can move the solution by O(1). ρ(T_J) ≈ 1 − 4.7e-10.

name: Jacobi diverges, Gauss–Seidel converges
description: A classic splitting example: ρ(T_J) = √5/2 ≈ 1.118 > 1, so Jacobi diverges, but ρ(T_GS) = 1/2, so Gauss–Seidel converges. Not diagonally dominant.

name: 4×4 nonsymmetric system
description: Nonsymmetric, strictly row diagonally dominant, κ₂ ≈ 3.15, with a complex pair of eigenvalues 5.5 ± 2.1i. CG does not apply; GMRES, LU and QR do.

name: Singular 3×3 system
description: rank A = 2 with null space span{(1, −2, 1)}. b = A·(1, 1, 1) is consistent, so there are infinitely many solutions (1, 1, 1) + t(1, −2, 1) and no unique one. Direct methods must report a zero pivot; the minimum-norm solution is (1, 1, 1).

name: Wyndor Glass Co.
description: Hillier & Lieberman, Introduction to Operations Research, §3.1: max 3x₁ + 5x₂ s.t. x₁ ≤ 4, 2x₂ ≤ 12, 3x₁ + 2x₂ ≤ 18. The origin is feasible.

name: Two-food diet
description: min 2x₁ + 3x₂ s.t. x₁ + x₂ ≥ 4, x₁ + 3x₂ ≥ 6, 2x₁ + x₂ ≥ 5 (written as ≤ rows with negative right-hand sides). The origin is infeasible, so the primal simplex needs phase 1 or big-M; the slack basis is dual feasible (c ≥ 0), so the dual simplex starts directly.

name: Degenerate vertex
description: max 2x₁ + x₂ s.t. x₁ + x₂ ≤ 4, x₁ − x₂ ≤ 2, x₁ ≤ 2. Three constraints meet at (2, 0), so the ratio test ties there; the simplex then makes a degenerate pivot (step length 0, basis changes, vertex does not) before it moves to (2, 2). Cycling needs m ≥ 2 rows and n − m ≥ 3 nonbasic columns in standard form (Marshall & Suurballe 1969); with 2 variables n − m = 2, so a 2-variable LP cannot cycle. See beale_cycling for a problem that does.

name: Beale's cycling example
description: Chvátal, Linear Programming (1983), p. 31 (after Beale 1955). With the largest-coefficient (Dantzig) entering rule and smallest-subscript tie-breaking in the ratio test the simplex method cycles through 6 degenerate bases; Bland's rule terminates.

name: Unbounded LP
description: Unbounded: max x₁ + x₂ s.t. −x₁ + x₂ ≤ 1, x₁ − 2x₂ ≤ 2. The feasible region contains the ray (4, 2) + t·(1, 1), t ≥ 0, along which the objective grows without bound.

name: Infeasible LP
description: Infeasible: x₁ + x₂ ≤ 2 and x₁ + x₂ ≥ 4 cannot both hold. Phase 1 ends with a positive sum of artificial variables (minimum 2).

name: Klee–Minty cube (n = 3)
description: Klee & Minty (1972) in Chvátal's form (Linear Programming, ch. 4): maximize $\sum_{j=1}^{n} 10^{n-j} x_j$ subject to $2\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} 10^{i-j} x_j + x_i \le 100^{i-1}$ for $i = 1, \dots, n$ and $\mathbf{x} \ge 0$. The Dantzig rule visits all $2^n = 8$ vertices (7 pivots) before it reaches the optimum.

name: Small transportation problem
description: Two suppliers (capacities 25, 30) and three customers (demands 10, 25, 15, met exactly) with unit costs [[8, 6, 10], [9, 12, 13]]. Six variables x₁₁…x₂₃, two ≤ rows and three equality rows.

name: Two-variable integer program
description: Winston, Operations Research (4th ed.), §9.3: max 8x₁ + 5x₂ s.t. x₁ + x₂ ≤ 6, 9x₁ + 5x₂ ≤ 45, x integer. The LP relaxation optimum is (3.75, 2.25) with value 41.25; the integer optimum is (5, 0) with value 40.

name: Three-variable integer program
description: max 4x₁ + 3x₂ + 3x₃ s.t. 4x₁ + 2x₂ + x₃ ≤ 10, 3x₁ + 4x₂ + 2x₃ ≤ 14, 2x₁ + x₂ + 3x₃ ≤ 7, x integer. LP relaxation: (1.2, 2.2, 0.8), value 13.8; integer optimum (1, 2, 1), value 13.

name: Square root of 2
description: The classic first example: a convex parabola with a simple root at √2.

name: Wallis' cubic
description: The equation Wallis used (1685) to present Newton's method; one real root near 2.0946.

name: cos x = x
description: The fixed point of cos (the Dottie number). f is decreasing, so the fixed-point iteration x ← x − λ f(x) needs λ < 0.

name: x¹⁰ − 1
description: Flat on the left and steep on the right of x = 1, so plain regula falsi keeps the right end fixed and converges slowly; Illinois-type methods fix this. Newton from x₀ = 0.5 overshoots to x ≈ 51.6.

name: Kepler's equation (e = 0.9)
latex: f(E) = E - e\sin E - M,\quad e = 0.9,\ M = 0.3
description: Eccentric anomaly E of an orbit with eccentricity e = 0.9 at mean anomaly M = 0.3. With the naive start E₀ = M, f′(E₀) = 1 − e cos M ≈ 0.14 is small and Newton's first step overshoots to E ≈ 2.2.

name: Double root
description: f touches zero at the double root x = 1 without a sign change, so no bracket can isolate it; Newton converges to it only linearly (rate ½). The default bracket isolates the simple root x = −2.

name: arctan x (Newton diverges)
description: Newton's method converges to 0 only for |x₀| < 1.3917452; from x₀ = 1.5 the iterates alternate in sign and grow without bound.

name: Newton 2-cycle
description: Newton from x₀ = 0 cycles 0 → 1 → 0 → … forever and never reaches the only real root x ≈ −1.769 (the cycle is superattracting because f″(0) = 0).

name: Steep exponential
description: Very steep on the right of the bracket (f(6) ≈ 393), so regula falsi keeps the right end and crawls; Newton from the left (x₀ < 0) jumps far to the right first.

name: Wilkinson polynomial (degree 5)
description: Five simple roots 1, …, 5; the default bracket holds all of them, so each bracketing method shows which root its own steps lead to. Evaluated in product form.

name: Quadratic
description: A convex parabola with minimizer x⋆ = 2 and f⋆ = 1. Parabolic interpolation and Newton's method are exact on it.

name: Tilted double well
description: Two wells: the global minimizer x ≈ −1.4730 (f ≈ −5.4442) and a local minimizer x ≈ 1.3470 (f ≈ −2.6186), separated by a local maximum at x ≈ 0.1260. f″ < 0 on |x| < √(2/3), where Newton's step points uphill.

name: Sine
description: One period of the sine. The interior minimizer is x⋆ = 3π/2 with f⋆ = −1; f″ = −sin x < 0 on (0, π), where Newton needs its safeguard.

name: x log x
description: The entropy-type function x ln x, convex on x > 0 with minimizer x⋆ = 1/e and f⋆ = −1/e. f′ → −∞ at 0; f is undefined (nan) for x < 0, so a long Newton step from x₀ ≥ 1 leaves the domain.

name: Shifted absolute value
description: Convex but not differentiable at the minimizer x⋆ = 0.3 (f⋆ = 0.045), because 0 ∈ ∂f(0.3) = [−0.7, 1.3]. Interval elimination still works; Newton's method oscillates between −1 and 1 because f′ jumps by 2 at the kink.

name: Sum of sines
description: Three local minima on [2.7, 7.5]; the global one is x ≈ 5.14574 with f ≈ −1.89960. f decreases at 2.7 and increases at 7.5, so every interval method ends at an interior local minimizer, but not necessarily the global one.

name: Flat valley
description: The minimizer x⋆ = 0 is infinitely flat: f and all its derivatives vanish there. In double precision f(x) underflows to exactly 0 for |x| < 0.0367, so no f-comparison can locate x⋆ better than that, and f′(x) < 10⁻⁸ already for |x| < 0.2. Newton's step x − 2x³/(4 − 6x²) converges sublinearly.

name: Rational model
description: A rational function of the kind a Padé or rational least-squares fit produces. On x > −1 it equals (x + 1) + 6/(x + 1) − 4, which is strictly convex with minimizer x⋆ = √6 − 1 ≈ 1.4495 and f⋆ = 2√6 − 4 ≈ 0.8990. It is asymmetric: steep on the left, nearly linear on the right.

name: Peak drug concentration
description: Plasma concentration after an oral dose (one-compartment model with first-order absorption). The peak is at t⋆ = ln(kₐ/kₑ)/(kₐ − kₑ) = ln 5/0.8 ≈ 2.0118 h with C ≈ 5.3499 mg/L. −C is convex only for t < 2t⋆ ≈ 4.02 h; beyond that Newton's step points the wrong way. (A nod to the legacy 'drug_effectiveness' example.)

name: Linear regression (2 parameters)
description: Fit a line to 200 noisy points. The loss is a quadratic bowl; the intercept and the slope are correlated because x is not centered (κ ≈ 6).

name: Logistic regression (2 parameters)
latex: f(w) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[\log(1 + e^{z_i}) - y_i z_i\right] + \frac{\lambda}{2}\|w\|^2,\ z_i = w_0 + w_1 x_i,\ \lambda = 10^{-2}
description: Classify 200 points on a line into two nearly separable classes. The ridge term λ = 10⁻² makes the minimizer unique; far from it the loss is almost linear, near it almost quadratic.

name: Ill-conditioned least squares
description: Two features on scales 1 and 30: the Hessian has κ ≈ 1070, a long narrow valley. Plain SGD must use a tiny step; per-coordinate methods (AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam) rescale the axes.

name: Huber regression (2 parameters)
latex: f(w) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} h_\delta(w_0 + w_1 x_i - y_i),\ h_\delta(r) = \begin{cases} \tfrac12 r^2 & |r| \le \delta \\ \delta(|r| - \tfrac12\delta) & |r| > \delta \end{cases},\ \delta = 1
description: A line fit with 10% gross outliers. The Huber loss is quadratic for small residuals and linear for large ones, so the outliers pull the fit far less than in least squares. f is convex and C¹ but its Hessian jumps.

name: Circle and line
description: The circle of radius 2 meets the line y = x − 1 in two points. J is singular where x + y = 0 (the line is tangent to a circle centered at 0 there).

name: Rosenbrock gradient = 0
description: Stationarity conditions of Rosenbrock's function: the only root is the minimizer (1, 1). J = ∇²f is singular on the parabola y = x² + 1/200.

name: Freudenstein–Roth
description: Moré–Garbow–Hillstrom test problem 2. The only root is (5, 4), but ½‖F‖² also has a non-zero local minimum near (11.41, −0.897), close to where J is singular (6y² − 8y − 12 = 0).

name: Trigonometric system
description: Two roots on the diagonal, at (π/6, π/6) and (5π/6, 5π/6). det J = sin(x + y) vanishes on the line x + y = π that separates them.

name: Two intersecting circles
description: Circles of radius 2 centered at (1, 0) and (−1, 1). det J = 4(1 − x − 2y) vanishes on the line through both centers, which separates the two roots.

name: Quadratic bowl
description: A well-conditioned convex quadratic (Hessian eigenvalues 2 and 4, condition number 2). Every descent method should converge quickly.

name: Ill-conditioned quadratic
description: A rotated convex quadratic with condition number 50: long, narrow, tilted elliptic contours. Steepest descent zig-zags; Newton converges in one step.

name: Random SPD quadratic (n = 20)
description: A 20-dimensional SPD quadratic A = H diag(λ) H, with H a Householder reflector and λ geometric from 1 to 100 (seeded with numopt.core.rng.Rng(20)).

name: Rosenbrock
description: Rosenbrock's banana valley (MGH problem 1, standard start (−1.2, 1)). Finding the valley is easy; following its curved floor to (1, 1) is hard.

name: Rosenbrock (n = 10)
description: The extended Rosenbrock function in 10 dimensions (the chained form used by scipy.optimize.rosen). Besides the global minimizer (1, …, 1) it has a local minimizer near (−1, 1, …, 1) (Shang & Qiu 2006 show this for 4 ≤ n ≤ 30).

name: Himmelblau
description: Himmelblau's function has four global minimizers, all with f = 0, and a local maximum near (−0.2708, −0.9230). Which minimizer a method finds depends on the start point.

name: Beale
description: Beale's function (MGH problem 5, standard start (1, 1)): flat plateaus and steep ridges near the corners of the box; global minimum f(3, 0.5) = 0.

name: Booth
description: Booth's function (J&Y 22): a convex quadratic with Hessian eigenvalues 2 and 18 (condition number 9).

name: Matyas
description: Matyas' function (J&Y 71): a convex quadratic whose Hessian eigenvalues are 0.04 and 1 (condition number 25), so the valley along y = x is very flat.

name: Three-hump camel
description: Three-hump camel (J&Y 29): a global minimum at the origin and two symmetric local minima (f ≈ 0.2986) separated by saddle points.

name: Six-hump camel
description: Six-hump camel (J&Y 30): two global minima f ≈ −1.0316 at ±(0.0898, −0.7127) and four local minima, in point-symmetric pairs.

name: Goldstein–Price
description: Goldstein–Price (J&Y 58): global minimum f(0, −1) = 3 and local minima f = 30, 84, 840; values span six orders of magnitude over the box.

name: Rastrigin
description: Rastrigin's function: a paraboloid covered by a regular grid of local minima near the integer points. Only the four local minima nearest the origin are listed; local methods stop in whichever basin they start.

name: Ackley
description: Ackley's function (J&Y 1): a nearly flat outer region with many local minima and a deep, narrow funnel at the origin. f has a cone-shaped kink at the origin; grad(0) returns the zero subgradient.

name: Styblinski–Tang
description: Styblinski–Tang (J&Y 144): separable; each coordinate has a deep and a shallow well, giving one global minimum (f ≈ −78.332) and three local minima.

name: McCormick
description: McCormick's function (J&Y 80) on its box [−1.5, 4] × [−3, 4]: global minimum f(−0.5472, −1.5472) = −π/3 − √3/2 ≈ −1.9132 over the box, and a local minimum at (2.5944, 1.5944). Unconstrained, f is unbounded below along x − y = 1 (f = σ/2 + sin σ with σ = x + y → −∞), so the global label holds on the box only.

name: Bohachevsky
description: Bohachevsky function 1 (J&Y 17): a convex bowl with cosine ripples that create many shallow local minima; global minimum f(0, 0) = 0.

name: Lévi N.13
description: Lévi function N.13: oscillating terms create rows of local minima around the global minimum f(1, 1) = 0.
